headline: Why Are Her Baby Pictures Under Surveillance?
lede:
Our right to a free and open Internets has been under threat lately. The NSA — btw, that stands for the National Security Agency, which has the fancy responsibility of analyzing and acting upon security data — has gotten into the habit of spying on Americans with no justification (including 12 spies who were using NSA tools to spy on their significant others). No, I'm not kidding.

The FCC — btw, that stands for the Federal Communications Commission, which is supposed to regulate and protect our communications channels — just made it easier for big companies to control the speed at which you are allowed to access particular websites. For example, your Internet company (i.e., Comcast or Verizon) could turn into a tiered pay system. So instead of being like a public utility where everyone gets the same amount of water or electricity, Verizon could give Netflix faster access for a fee, but then the smaller start-up that wants to compete and couldn't afford it would get slower access.

The Internet has become one of the most important resources in our lives. It's a shared resource that all of us take part in. Government spying on it, and corporate interference in it are probably not things we want for the future. So Mozilla had some children voice concern for their own future. Because it's kind of important. What kind of web do you want?

headline: Stephen Colbert Calls Out Cable News On Their Inability To Report Actual News
lede:
Being a 24 hour news station is hard. You have find ways to fill 24 hours of airtime without being redundant and without there being breaking news every single day. For CNN, it's even tougher, because their bosses don't actually care about news quality, they care about ratings. They generally just let shrill politically partisan people scream past each other for half the day without fact checking them, and the other half, they underfund their actual reporters and do no long term investigative journalism. Instead, they find something sensationalist to milk and hype until it's been beaten to death with the tedious cudgel that is Wolf Blitzer's beard of indifference.

Stephen Colbert decided to get to the bottom of their latest non-story, the story of if there was any story left about the tragedy on the crash of a Malaysian Airlines plane. He nails it.

headline: This Dad Has A Message To The Boys Who Want To Date His Daughter. ADDENDUM: Also, The Girls.
lede:

There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. So I want to acknowledge that I'm aware of my rampant hypocrisy. I'm a dad. I'm a jackass. I'm learning how to fight it and hold myself to a higher standard.

Which brings me to Jesse Parent, a dad who says all the things that probably every parent has dealt with thinking all their lives. At 1:50, he disables his lizard brain. And at 2:42, he makes up for his first 2 minutes. Hilariously.

headline: Dads Often Judge Their Sons And Daughters Differently. He Says It Out-Loud. Then Redeems Himself.
lede:
DISCLOSURE: I have a daughter. Someday, she will grow up and become a young woman , and probably want to date people. There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. So I want to acknowledge that I'm aware of my rampant hypocrisy. I'm a dad. I'm a jackass. I'm learning how to fight it and hold myself to a higher standard.

Which brings me to Jesse Parent, a dad who says all the things that probably every parent has dealt with thinking all their lives. At 1:50, he disables his lizard brain. And at 2:42, he makes up for his first 2 minutes. Hilariously.

headline: Economist Paul Krugman Lays Out The Basics Of Why Everybody’s In A World Of Hurt Except For The 1%
lede:
A few definitions to tee this up:

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was very much run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

headline: What Do Real Women Look Like After They Give Birth? Like This.
lede:
After giving birth to her son Sequoia, Jade Baell posted photos of her post-birth body to show the world what a real mother's body looks like.

What happened next was remarkable.

The photo went viral, and something struck Jade: she realised mothers across the world so rarely see themselves reflected accurately in the media. She was flooded with hundreds and thousands of messages from women telling their story about their bodies, how they struggled with not fitting the norm of 'beautiful' and how they felt her photo helped redefine beauty.

Jade proceeded to photograph hundreds of mothers who used to feel 'too saggy', 'too wrinkly' 'too fat', but who now are being celebrated for who they are by Jade and her project. Watch her video below to hear more.

headline: Hobby Lobby To Female Employees: No Birth Control For You. We Only Use It To Make Money.
lede:
Hobby Lobby does not want to indirectly provide birth control to its employees via its health plan. In fact, the company has been so adamant about its position, which it claims is based on religious grounds, that it took its case all the way to the Supreme Court.

As it turns out, Hobby Lobby's retirement plan had more than $73 million invested in mutual funds that had stakes in... wait for it... manufacturers of contraceptive products like, you know, Plan B (the "morning after" pill), IUDs, and birth control pills.

Apparently, Hobby Lobby does not want anything to do with providing its female employees who wish to control their own fertility with a very basic and important tool like the birth control pill. But the company is willing to look the other way then said birth control items are good for the bottom line.

Where I'm from (planet earth), we call that hypocrisy.

headline: Stephen Colbert Calls Out Cable News On Their Inability To Report Actual News
lede:
Being a 24 hour news station is hard. You have find ways to fill 24 hours of airtime without being redundant and without there being breaking news every single day. For CNN, it's even tougher, because their bosses don't actually care about news quality, they care about ratings. They generally just let shrill politically partisan people scream past each other for half the day without fact checking them, and the other half, they underfund their actual reporters and do no long term investigative journalism. Instead, they find something sensationalist to milk and hype until it's been beaten to death with the tedious cudgel that is Wolf Blitzer's beard of indifference.

Stephen Colbert decided to get to the bottom of their latest non-story, the story of if there was any story left about the tragedy on the crash of a Malaysian Airlines plane. He nails it.

headline: Usually, Art Is All About Those In Power. Not For This Guy.
lede:
Ralph Fasanella was born on Labor Day, 1914. He was the son of an Italian immigrant, and one of his first jobs was slinging ice back in the days when "icebox" meant refrigerator ... with a block of ice. He went on to work in a factory and as a truck driver, and then became a union organizer.

That was before he became a fascinating painter. He often used large canvasses, because he envisioned his work to be in union halls, rather than, as he said, “to hang in some rich guy’s living room.” Some of his paintings were about common working people; others, about strikes, civil unrest, JFK's assasination, and other relics of the times.

His works are on display right now at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, DC, and a parallel exhibit is also happening in the lobby of the AFL-CIO building. More on that below the images.

headline: Usually, Art Is All About Those In Power. Not For One Amazing Painter.
lede:
Ralph Fasanella was born on Labor Day, 1914. He was the son of an Italian immigrant, and one of his first jobs was slinging ice back in the days when "icebox" meant refrigerator ... with a block of ice. He went on to work in a factory and as a truck driver, and then became a union organizer.

That was before he became a fascinating painter. He often used large canvasses, because he envisioned his work to be in union halls, rather than, as he said, “to hang in some rich guy’s living room.” Some of his paintings were about common working people; others, about strikes, civil unrest, JFK's assasination, and other relics of the times.

His works are on display right now at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, DC, and a parallel exhibit is also happening in the lobby of the AFL-CIO building. More on that below the images.

headline: Hobby Lobby To Female Employees: No Birth Control For You. We Only Use It To Make Money.
lede:

As it turns out, Hobby Lobby's retirement plan had more than $73 million invested in mutual funds that had stakes in... wait for it... manufacturers of contraceptive products like, you know, Plan B (the "morning after" pill), IUDs, and birth control pills.

Apparently, Hobby Lobby does not want anything to do with providing its female employees who wish to control their own fertility with a very basic and important tool like the birth control pill. This clip is from the 2009 inauguration ceremony of newly-elected President Obama. Pete Seeger came to play a little music with Bruce Springsteen, Seeger’s grandson Tao, and many others. Originally written by Woody Guthrie, who Seeger performed with many times, it’s a powerful version of “This Land Is Your Land,” with lyrics (including the frequently-forgotten last few stanzas!) below the video. headline: Usually, Art Represents The Culture Of Those In Power. Not For This Guy.
lede:
Ralph Fasanella was born on Labor Day, 1914. He was the son of an Italian immigrant, and one of his first jobs was slinging ice back in the days when "icebox" meant refrigerator ... with a block of ice. He went on to work in a factory and as a truck driver, and then became a union organizer.

That was before he became a fascinating painter. He often used large canvasses, because he envisioned his work to be in union halls, rather than, as he said, “to hang in some rich guy’s living room.” Some of his paintings were about common working people; others, about strikes, civil unrest, JFK's assasination, and other relics of the times.

His works are on display right now at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, DC, and a parallel exhibit is also happening in the lobby of the AFL-CIO building. More on that below the images.

headline: Banksy Has Updated His Famous 'The Girl With The Balloon' Artwork To Stand With Syria
lede:
The Syria crisis hasn't slowed down, and over 100,000 people have died in three years, with thousands of mostly women and children displaced.

But people are standing with Syria, including the street artist Banksy who has re-worked his famous and popular art work of a girl reaching for a red balloon with the intention of shedding light on the Syrian crisis. The original artwork depicted a young girl with flowing hair, with a heart shaped balloon just beyond her grasp — the new re-working of his classic stencil is of a young Syrian girl accompanied with a #WithSyria hashtag.

See the creative way Banksy is using his famous platform to draw attention to the ongoing crisis in the image, as well as photographs of young Syrian children holding a red balloon as part of the #WithSyria campaign. BONUS: Idris Elba supports the campaign and is in a photo below, too.

headline: Here's What Morgan Freeman Had To Say About Racism And Here's A Guy Explaining What He Got Wrong
lede: I've encountered far too many people who think the solution to racism is to just ignore it. Which...makes no sense! Ignoring a problem won't make it go away. Sadly, actor Morgan Freeman co-signed this idea in an interview a few years ago, which has only helped keep the myth alive. Here's the thing. Morgan Freeman is totally entitled to his opinion, even though I don't agree with him. Every black person is going to have a different opinion/experience/perspective when it comes to racism. With that being said, it's important to be careful when it comes to using "my black friend said" or in this case "this black celebrity said" to dismiss someone else's experience/beliefs. headline: Hobby Lobby To Female Employees: No Birth Control For You. We Only Use It To Make Money.
lede:
Hobby Lobby does not want to indirectly provide birth control to its employees via its health plan. In fact, the company has been so adamant about its position, which it claims is based on religious grounds, that it took its case all the way to the Supreme Court.

As it turns out, Hobby Lobby's retirement plan had more than $73 million invested in mutual funds that had stakes in... wait for it... manufacturers of contraceptive products like, you know, Plan B (the "morning after" pill), IUDs, and birth control pills.

Apparently, Hobby Lobby does not want anything to do with providing its female employees who wish to control their own fertility with a very basic and important tool like the birth control pill. But the company is willing to look the other way then said birth control items are good for the bottom line.

Where I'm from (planet earth), we call that hypocrisy.

headline: Banksy Has Updated His Famous 'The Girl With The Balloon' Artwork To Stand With Syria
lede:
The Syria crisis hasn't slowed down, and over 100,000 people have died in three years, with thousands of Syrian's displaced, many of whom are women and children.

But many people are still standing with Syria, including the street artist Banksy who has re-worked his famous and popular art work of a girl reaching for a red balloon with the intention of shedding light on the Syrian crisis. The original artwork depicted a young girl with flowing hair with a heart shaped balloon just beyond her grasp — the new re-working of his classic stencil is of a young Syrian girl accompanied with a #WithSyria hashtag, which is part of a global vigil campaign today to mark the three years since the crisis began.

Have a look at the following below:

1. Banky's original artwork alongside Banksy's new re-worked image, and his website message in support of #WithSyria

2. Photographs of young Syrian children holding red balloons as part of the #WithSyria campaign

3. A photograph of actor Idris Elba with a red balloon supporting the campaign

4. The animated campaign video for #WithSyria with Idrsi Elba narrating and music by the band Elbow

headline: Why Does It Matter That Some Children Hear More Words Than Others?
lede: Did you know that the learning process for kids starts way before kindergarten? And before pre-school too? Babies are actually learning all the time, so how we talk to them is really important, because it is literally helping their brains grow! Unfortunately, kids born in poverty often do not get the interaction needed to promote that kind of brain growth, and as a result end up hearing on average 30 million fewer words in their earliest years compared to kids born into wealthier families. It's a real shame that something so far beyond their control puts these kids at a disadvantage before they even put on their first-day-of-school outfit. Here's a look at the science behind it and how we can help all of our little ones succeed!

lede: So much education for at-risk teens focuses on what not to do--don't do drugs, don't have sex, don't drop out. The D3 Lab focuses on giving them tools for positive change. headline: What Is MayOne, And Why Is The Internet Freaking Out About It?
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: Meet The Harvard Professor With A Brilliant Plan To Tackle Money In Politics
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: Usually, Art Is About Those In Power. Not For This Guy.
lede:
Ralph Fasanella was born on Labor Day, 1914. He was the son of an Italian immigrant, and one of his first jobs was slinging ice back in the days when "icebox" meant refrigerator ... with a block of ice. He went on to work in a factory and as a truck driver, and then became a union organizer.

That was before he became a fascinating painter. He often used large canvasses, because he envisioned his work to be in union halls, rather than, as he said, “to hang in some rich guy’s living room.” Some of his paintings were about common working people; others, about strikes, civil unrest, JFK's assasination, and other relics of the times.

His works are on display right now at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, DC, and a parallel exhibit is also happening in the lobby of the AFL-CIO building. More on that below the images.

headline: The Story Of How A Hashtag Grew Into The Beginnings Of A Huge Movement
lede:

The hashtag #YesAllWomen was born, and it absolutely took Twitter by storm; millions of Tweets have gone out with that hashtag.

I have read literally hundreds of them if not more, and I can tell you they are chilling. When I mentioned the hashtag and some of the stories to my wife, she replied, "Of course...I always carry my keys in a way that they can be used if someone attacks me. We learn that early on." For someone who considers himself a pretty well educated and in-touch dude, it rather floored me.

Here is a map of the Tweets from around the world, and two of my favorite Tweets, but there are so many more of these conversations happening right now on Twitter; link to get there is below.

headline: Brilliant: A Crowdfunded Super PAC to Take Down Corrupt Politicians
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: There’s A Huge Storm On Twitter, And It Was Started By The Hashtag #YesAllWomen
lede:
One very mentally ill young man who blamed women for his failure to actually get dates and get along with women killed 6 people and wounded 7 more. The Internet responded in a huge way, and it's still actually doing so right now. The hashtag #YesAllWomen was born, and it absolutely took Twitter by storm; millions of Tweets have gone out with that hashtag.

I have read literally hundreds of them if not more, and I can tell you they are chilling. When I mentioned the hashtag and some of the stories to my wife, she replied, "Of course...I always carry my keys in a way that they can be used if someone attacks me. We learn that early on." For someone who considers himself a pretty well educated and in-touch dude, it rather floored me.

Here is a map of the Tweets from around the world, and two of my favorite Tweets, but there are so many more of these conversations happening right now on Twitter; link to get there is below.

headline: Fed Up With Money In Politics? You're Going To Love This One.
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: Rich Kids Getting Financial Aid From Colleges Is The Single Most Annoying Thing I've Learned Today
lede:

While I learned so much at my four years at Rhode Island School of Design, the tuition costs to go there are staggering (which frankly, is an understatement). The financial aid I received from RISD in addition to federal grants were much-welcomed silver linings, and I was able to attend, albeit with a debt-friend that will follow me around for a couple decades.

Marian Wang wonders: What happens, though, when a student is deemed "not worthy" of financial aid?

headline: Eating Healthy Is Challenging As Is. Now Imagine You Only Had $4 To Do It.
lede: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP or food stamps, helps low and no income people in the US purchase food. Sounds awesome right? The downside is a days worth of food stamps is only about $4, whiiiich isn't very much money. So grad student Leanne Brown created a cookbook that shows how to stretch that $4 to create a variety of healthy and delicious meals! Just thinking of all the people who are going to benefit from this book, makes me love the project even more.

headline: Watching A Black Woman Smile In The Face Of Racism Is Pure Delight. Then She Goes In For The Hug…
lede: Mo Asumang is a German TV host and filmmaker, and what she pulls off in this video is amazing. Not only does Mo speak with groups of people who claim to hate her (which she does with grace and compassion), but she actually gets a few of them to let down their guard and reveal that they might just have a heart. It's fascinating to witness and probably the one and only context in which you can root for a racist — for them to stop being racist!

headline: It's Pretty Terrifying That Such A Huge And Devastating Project Can Be Proposed Without Us Noticing
lede:
There's an island in Southeast Asia called Borneo. Heard of it? It's actually the 3rd largest island in the world. It's home to one of the oldest and most biodiverse rainforests in existence, with multiple endangered and endemic species and hundreds of new species identified in the past 20 years (including an unknown mammal called the Bornean red carnivore, the thought of which is probably gonna give me nightmares).

Borneo is also the site of a proposed hydroelectric mega-dam. And that, my friends, is what the project below is all about. Don't miss the part at 2:00 where they talk about the film project itself.

lede: 99% of women between the ages of 15 and 44 who are sexually active have used birth control at some point. That's a lot, but can we go back to the words "sexually active" for a sec? They often get glossed over to focus on who supports birth control, or other reasons why women use it (and there are plenty of them, don't get me wrong!). But why can't we talk about sex? I love this cartoon for taking the taboo subject of sex – and the slut-shaming that comes with it – and knocking it right over.

headline: When Pharrell Wrote The Song, ‘Happy,’ I’m Pretty Sure This Is Exactly What He Had In Mind​
lede: When you spend all day coaching little league, teaching ballet, feeding the hungry, building bike trails or planting the community garden only to hear people turn around and diss your hometown, you're bound to get a little mad. lede:

headline: You Want To Know The Truth About Vaccines And Autism? Can You Handle The Horrible Truth? You Sure?
lede:
Once upon a time, a scientist named Dr. Andrew Wakefield published in the medical journal "Lancet" that he had discovered a link between autism and vaccines. After years of controversy and making parents mistrust vaccines, along with collecting $674,000 from lawyers who would benefit from suing vaccine makers, it was discovered that he had made the whole thing up. The Lancet publicly apologized and reported that further investigation led to the discovery that he had fabricated everything.

In the intervening years, millions have been spent on studying this further to see if there was anything that could connect autism and vaccines. This is what they found.

headline: A Girl Takes A Walk, And The Whole World Feels Entitled To An Opinion
lede: The guys in this comic need to take a fast trip to a very far away planet (and that's the kindest thing I can say), but they’re just on the extreme end of a spectrum of put-downs constantly thrown at people of a certain larger body shape and size. This kind of harassment can be a casual comment that comes from a well-intentioned person making an erroneous connection between health and weight, or it can be some of the heinously degrading things depicted below, or it can even be something as seemingly innocuous as a fat joke. What happens after years and years of hearing comments like that? For folks like the author of this comic it's totally dehumanizing — being thought of as a body and not as a person — and some days it's so bad even SHE can't see herself beyond how the rest of the world sees her. Fat is not a personality type. Fat should not be an insult. Fat is an adjective. Full stop. So next time you hear a fat joke, or someone makes a comment about someone else's weight, or judges a person for their weight first and personality second, remember this comic. And tell them they're wrong. Because no one deserves to feel less than human.

headline: The Ridiculous Future Awfulness That Hobby Lobby And The Supreme Court Have Created
lede:
Hobby Lobby is suing for the right to prevent their health insurance from covering things like birth control. The Supreme Court (as of March 2014) is hearing oral arguments on the matter. So here's a fake clip from the future to explain why this just might be a bad idea.

Update 6/30/14: Well, the Supreme Court went ahead and declared that privately held corporations are religious people. Supreme Court Justice Judith Ginsburg wrote a scathing dissent of the decision, saying, "The absence of such precedent is just what one would expect, for the exercise of religion is characteristic of natural persons, not artificial legal entities."

headline: How And Why We Use 'Sorry' Fuels Gender Stereotypes, And This Shampoo Ad Calls It Out
lede:
There’s nothing wrong with apologizing. In fact, it’s sort of what you’re supposed to do when you’re in the wrong. However, studies show that women are more likely to apologize for non-offensive behavior than men… Which unfortunately fuels the double-standard that women who aren’t “apologetic enough” are bossy (...or worse).

So, ladies and gentlemen. I’m not here to tell you how to use your words... That would be silly. But I am here to show you this video, in hopes that we might recognize this behavior in ourselves and work together to create a world in which these sorts of apologies aren’t expected from either gender.

headline: Hobby Lobby Gets What It Wants And John Oliver Gives It What It Deserves To Get
lede:
The Supreme Court ruled that Hobby Lobby (a company whose 401k plan includes investments in the companies that produce the very drugs it's suing to not cover) is free to discriminate against women and not cover birth control, which — aside from being used for sex — is also used to treat endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome and eases cramps, smooths out skin, helps with anemia, helps protect women from pelvic inflammatory disease, and reduces the risks of some cancers. In its ruling, it's basically stated that private businesses (public businesses still have to be decent human being corporate entities) can interfere with their employee's reproductive health.

John Oliver has an opinion about that. Especially at 3:40.

headline: If You're In The Middle Of The US Wealth Distribution, Here's What You Look Like Next To The Top 1%

headline: The Number 721 And What It Means To Restaurant CEOs
lede: Restaurant CEOs now make 721 times the minimum wage workers who comprise most of their workforce. Up from 609 times in 2006. And this is assuming flat-out minimum wage; in those restaurants where workers depend on tips to survive, the minimum is much less and has remained so for decades. So ... do these CEOs deserve that much more?

headline: 30 Seconds Of Women Over-Apologizing, Followed By 30 Seconds Of Them *So* Destroying That Stereotype
lede:
There’s nothing wrong with apologizing. In fact, it’s sort of what you’re supposed to do when you’re in the wrong. However, studies* show that women are more likely to apologize for inoffensive behavior than men, which unfortunately fuels the double standard that women who aren’t “apologetic enough” are bossy (or worse).

So, ladies and gentlemen, I’m not here to tell you how to use your words. That would be silly. But I am here to show you this video in hopes that we might recognize this behavior in ourselves and work together to create a world in which over apologizing isn't expected from either gender.

headline: What’s Ratchet? And Why Does The Word Need To Die Like Right Now?
lede:
It’s hard when people think they know you because they saw someone who ‘looked just like you,’ on TV. Then you’ve got to go through the trouble of re-introducing yourself, so they can unlearn what they’ve seen. Just because that black lady turned over a table and threw a glass of champagne on her friend’s face, doesn’t mean I will. I mean really, can’t we all just get along?

This video tries to explain that. At 2:58 she sheds light on a little term that’s hurting lots of women.

headline: Being A Soldier Is Hard Enough Without The Top Brass Not Protecting You From Sexual Assault
lede:
Olivia Gatwood was sitting in the airport one day, when she heard a bunch of troubling stories on CNN about female soldiers and what they go through when they are sexually assaulted. In the civilian world, things can be hard enough when you are attacked. In the military world, the struggle can be far worse. Their stories are often covered up, they are dismissed and often booted from the military they volunteered to join while the perpetrator remains. So she wrote a piece about it. This is the story that women in the military know far too well.

TRIGGER WARNING: She talks about assaults and the coverups that occur after.

headline: These 2 Minutes Of Frozen-In-Motion LEGO People Drilled Into My Heart And Struck Anger. A Lot Of It.
lede:
Think of your favorite toy from childhood. What color was it? Now think of that toy if it were sponsored by the first giant corporation that comes to mind. With all that branding, the company (and it's colors) become part of the toy itself. I gotta say, the idea that kids would grow up with the same fond memories I have for Pogs and Teddy Ruxpin for an oil corporation making use of the Halo effect? Very unnerving.

Is a toy with a big sponsored logo on it still a toy? Or is it a tool?

headline: The Hard Truth About Being A Female Soldier In Our Military Is Really Hard To Believe. And True.
lede:
Olivia Gatwood was sitting in the airport one day, when she heard a bunch of troubling stories on CNN about female soldiers and what they go through when they are sexually assaulted. In the civilian world, things can be hard enough when you are attacked. In the military world, the struggle can be far worse. Their stories are often covered up, they are dismissed and often booted from the military they volunteered to join while the perpetrator remains. So she wrote a piece about it. This is the story that too many women in the military know far too well.

TRIGGER WARNING: She talks about assaults and the coverups that occur after.

headline: Policemen Didn't Care, Politicians Did Nothing; So He Wrote A Song Catchy Enough To Make You Notice
lede:
The American economy has gotten so weird that people are now knocking down houses — not building them – to make money. And this guy has a really unique, catchy way of explaining what's going down.

Basically, it’s now more profitable in most American cities (if not altogether legal, but that's another thing) to strip buildings and sell them for parts — but it’s not like recycling. It’s more like a systematic destruction of historic neighborhoods for profit. Profit wins, destruction happens, humans lose, and history is sad.

And at the end, you can even hear that the buncha swiss people he’s performing for get riled up. Don't forget that Swiss people are famously neutral people, guys! So ….won’t somebody please do something about the brick thieves?

headline: The Awful Things Some Officers Tell Women Soldiers After They've Been Assaulted By Male Soldiers
lede:
Olivia Gatwood was sitting in the airport one day, when she heard a bunch of troubling stories on CNN about female soldiers and what they go through when they are sexually assaulted. In the civilian world, things can be hard enough when you are attacked. In the military world, the struggle can be far worse. Their stories are often covered up, they are dismissed and often booted from the military they volunteered to join while the perpetrator remains. So she wrote a piece about it. This is the story that too many women in the military know far too well.

TRIGGER WARNING: She talks about assaults and the coverups that occur after.

The reality of the movement, and particularly the summer of 1964, is both more mundane and more tragic. It's filled with volunteers who grindingly pounded the pavement to organize voter registration and careful prepared for the violence that was sure to follow.

Check out some very rare footage of that summer and the story of 3 missing volunteers that shook a nation out of its convenient apathy.

lede:

headline: Two Teenagers Destroyed Countless Families. These Guys Rewinded The Tape To Try To Answer Why.
lede:
Jamie and Geoff do writing workshops all over the country, in prisons, juvenile halls, and high schools, seeking out the kids who have no outlet to express their rage and pain. From their work, they wrote a play called, "In Spite Of Everything" which toured around the globe and brought people together to discuss the very uniquely horrific American tragedy that is school shootings. And from that play came this story.

Eric Klebold and Dylan Harris had 3 months left of school. Dylan had been accepted into a college program. There was a moment they could have called it all off and went on like nothing happened. But they didn't. They crossed the line no one should cross. Columbine was a horrific tragedy that made a lasting impact on America. It woke us all up, it made us realize there really was evil in the world, and it shook us to the core. Growing up in Colorado, I couldn't have ever imagined anyone doing this. And yet it happened. And all the adults missed it. And none of us could fathom why or how it was even possible.

Jamie DeWolf and Geoff Trenchard had fantasies like Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris growing up, too. Hell, any kid who was having a rough go would occasionally imagine what they'd do if they could. I know I did. But it never occurred to me to actually take any action. It was just fantasy. So what made them different? What made them say, "Lets go all the way with this"?

Jamie and Geoff tried to find out. They wanted to give a voice to alienated kids who don't make the horrible choices Dylan and Eric made. They wanted to discover what drove these kids to such angry places and find a healthy outlet to help kids like them survive.

They say some pretty shocking things in this, but I urge you to listen all the way through. It's pretty damn poignant.

TRIGGER WARNING: This reenacts the tragic and violent events of that day, and includes shootings and violence.

headline: Ever Notice How Hollywood Makes Certain Kinds Of People Extinct In Apocalyptic Movies?
lede:
I want you to think for a moment about romantic characters in Science Fiction movies. They all pretty much follow a certain archetype, right? Han Solo and Princess Leia, Lois Lane and Clark Kent, Doctor Who and River Song follow a seemingly very strict "straight-people-only" template. Think about it: even Ann Darrow and King Kong had romantic chemistry.

For for a nerd that happened to like boys (like me), this was especially disheartening growing up. Seeing people who are like you immortalised in television and movies helps shape how you relate to the rest of the world. It's troubling that a genre like science fiction has been ignoring the laws of humanity, too. At least, till now.

headline: Alabama Celebrates A Confederate Holiday On Martin Luther King Day. Yup.
lede:
I'm a war veteran, a Southerner, and an African American and everything inside me cries out in pain that almost every state in the South still celebrates a Confederate holiday. As a veteran, I can understand the noble desire to honor those who heard their country's call and paid the ultimate price, but that's what Memorial Day is for.

Don't get me wrong, I have a ton of Southern pride. There are so many things to be proud of: our music, our food (oh, the FOOD!), our architecture, our hospitality... But I can't be proud that so many states celebrate fighting a war in order to keep people like me in chains – and spend tax dollars to do it.
share_text: Let's say it doesn't make this Southerner proud... not at all.

headline: A Guy Explains That 4 Of 6700 Banks Are Not Hurting Families. The Senator Responds Correctly.
lede:
When you file for bankruptcy, you can often get debt forgiven or restructured. But if you have student loans, some nice lobbyists have made sure they are not part of that deal. A mom with $100k in student loan debt died, and her children went into the care of their grandparents, who were then saddled with their dead child's debt and had no way to get the debt forgiven.

Senator Warren decided to ask one of the top lobbyists who run a consumer bank lobbying organization (for the banks, not the consumers) how and when he's going to fix that. It didn't go well for the banker. Especially at 5:20.

Now that you've thought about it, listen to Zerlina Maxwell do a talk on how we can help solve the problem. A lot of messaging focuses on blaming the victim. Yet, when cities like Vancouver actively ran campaigns to tell guys what constitutes rape, they decreased sexual assault by 10% in 1 year. Education is key. And Zerlina is hear to educate you.

headline: Robin Williams' Advice For People Who Are Depressed Is Really Good
lede:
There's been a quote going around attributed to Robin Williams that goes as follows: "You're only given a little spark of madness. You mustn't lose it." Here's where it came from. He was performing at the Roxy in 1978 for a brand new comedy special on a little known network called HBO. In the audience were a surprising group of people. Henry Winkler (The Fonz), Tony Danza before he was famous, and even John Ritter whom he does a weird round of improv with at the end of this video.

I've included just the moment that sort of kept me sane as a kid. It helped me justify how weird I was. It's a delightful 5 minutes. If you'd like to watch the whole special, excerpts of which were used to create his first album, "Reality... What A Concept" you can start it from the beginning.

headline: Have You Ever Heard Of The Ludlow Massacre? Here’s Your Chance.
lede:
It was a time of great social upheaval in our country. During the years leading up to the Ludlow Massacre, miners all around the country looking to make a better life for themselves and their families setup picket lines, organized massive parades and rallies, and even took up arms. Some died.

I always wondered why history like this was never taught in school when I grew up. Could it be that the powers that be would rather keep this kind of thing under wraps?

headline: One Of The First Movies To Talk About Being Gay Didn't Even Talk About Being Gay
lede:
In 1961, Shirley Maclaine and Audrey Hepburn starred in The Children's Hour. While censorship guidelines at the time of filming didn't outrightly prohibit the mention of homosexuality, it was widely know that the topic was not something that was acceptable to discuss on the big screen.

At 2:20, you'll see the pain that came with Shirley Maclaine's character's struggle. As one of the first movies to broach this topic, you'll be very surprised to hear what she says at 2:50 and Susie Bright's insight at the end painfully illustrates the things our society still needs to work on.

headline: Lauryn Hill Rewrote The Lyrics To A Song In ’The Sound Of Music’. It’s My New Favorite Thing.
lede:
Singer Lauryn Hill wrote a song called "Black Rage" in 2012, but recently released it on music sharing site Soundcloud and dedicated it to the town of Ferguson. On her Tumblr, she writes:

An old sketch of Black Rage, done in my living room. Strange, the course of things. Peace for MO.

It's a reimagining of "My Favorite Things" from American classic movie "The Sound of Music". It's really stirring, as much as the original, but for totally different reasons.

headline: Maybe They Think It's OK To Abuse Them Because They Aren't REAL Women?
lede:
I'm an unabashed nerd. Most prominent in my repertoire of nerdery is video games. But video games haven't always been good to me. Female characters are routinely verbally and physically abused, sexually assaulted, and killed in video games. I'm always annoyed by unnecessarily revealing costumes and obnoxiously gigantic boobs, but it's the violence against female characters that keeps me away from certain games – even entire genres.

This video starts with a long series of graphic examples of unnecessary violence against women from 28 of the most successful video games of the last eight years*, but I'm starting you toward the end (23:30) where Anita Sarkeesian discusses an example of a video that does "abuse as a theme" right and why it's important (and possible) for video games to be violent without being harmful.

Quick vocab lesson before you start: "NPC" means "non-playable character".

If you start at 23:30 then there are no descriptions or depictions of violence, but if you start at the beginning instead – trigger warning like all get out for everything I mentioned above.

headline: Women Can Look So Life-Like In Video Games. So Can The Way They Get Beaten To Death.
lede:
I'm an unabashed nerd. Most prominent in my repertoire of nerdery is video games. But video games haven't always been good to me. Female characters are routinely verbally and physically abused, sexually assaulted, and killed in video games. I'm always annoyed by unnecessarily revealing costumes and obnoxiously gigantic boobs, but it's the violence against female characters that keeps me away from certain games – even entire genres.

This video starts with a long series of graphic examples of unnecessary violence against women from 28 of the most successful video games of the last eight years*, but I'm starting you toward the end (23:30) where Anita Sarkeesian discusses an example of a video that does "abuse as a theme" right and why it's important (and possible) for video games to be violent without being harmful.

Quick vocab lesson before you start: "NPC" means "non-playable character".

If you start at 23:30 then there are no descriptions or depictions of violence, but if you start at the beginning instead – trigger warning like all get out for everything I mentioned above.

headline: Don't Judge The Gross Things This Guy Says About Love Until You Hear What He Says At 1:40
lede:
After my dad was diagnosed with Pancreatic cancer, we had to have the painful conversation about his funeral. His body had been ravaged by chemo and and weight loss, his skin hung a little lower on his face, and he was adamant that he not have a funeral at all. He was not a fan of people saying posthumous things about what an amazing man he was when most of the things he did in life were not that amazing (his words, not mine.) At that point, all of us rolled our eyes at him, and as gallows humor is required when you are looking death in the eye, one of us responded, "No offense dad, but your funeral isn't for you. So suck it up."

Which leads me to a video about why love is important in dark times. Brace yourselves, Jesse Parent is about about to talk about farting. If you trust my judgement in any way, I urge you to withhold judgement till at least 1:40. Because this is beautiful.

headline: A Guy Decided To Make A Serious Dramatic Movie About Civil Unrest In Iran. His Name? Jon Stewart.
lede:
Jon Stewart, host of the Daily Show, along with being one of my favorite people when it comes to speaking truth to power, also took a summer off last year to go shoot a movie. Not star in it, but actually write and direct it. It's not a comedy.

It's based on the true story of Maziar Bahari, a Canadian journalist who was born in Iran, and covered Iranian elections in 2009 for Newsweek during the Arab Spring. He ended up witnessing the election and shooting footage that got sent to the BBC. The police arrested him, and tortured and interrogated him for 118 days.

This is the trailer for that movie, Rosewater. And my eyes teared up a little. So apparently I'm not all dead inside.

headline: People Spend 16 Minutes Every Day Doing Something They Think Is Good. It Ain't.
lede:

I'm afraid I'm showing my age, because thanks to efficient electric ignitions in today's vehicles, idling a car for just 10 seconds burns more fuel than restarting it. The facts are simple, and the solution is elegant!

Check out these easy-on-the-eyes figures, and share this with everyone in your carpool. If they're not into saving 40,000 tons of CO2, maybe they'd be into saving up to a couple hundred bucks a year in gas money.

headline: If You Can't Do This In The Bedroom, You Might As Well Break Up With Your Partner Now
lede:
After my dad was diagnosed with Pancreatic cancer, we had to have the painful conversation about his funeral. His body had been ravaged by chemo and and weight loss, his skin hung a little lower on his face, and he was adamant that he not have a funeral at all. He was not a fan of people saying posthumous things about what an amazing man he was when most of the things he did in life were not that amazing (his words, not mine.) At that point, all of us rolled our eyes at him, and as gallows humor is required when you are looking death in the eye, one of us responded, "No offense dad, but your funeral isn't for you. So suck it up."

Which leads me to a video about why love is important in dark times. Brace yourselves, Jesse Parent is about about to talk about farting. If you trust my judgement in any way, I urge you to withhold judgement till at least 1:40. Because this is beautiful.

headline: A Man Ran 70 Miles For A Cause He Was Passionate About
lede:
So, my activism is pretty lazy, I hafta admit. I mostly sit in front of this computer and spew stuff I believe in. This guy, Nick Triolo, is a teensy bit more energetic than I am. OK, he's a badass.

He was pissed about the development of an open-pit mine in a beautiful area of Mexico, so he did something about it. Something I could never do. He ran. Seventy miles in one day, to be exact.

He got lots of attention for the cause, and even made this film about it to spread the word. Doesn't it make you wonder what you could do for the causes you're passionate about?

So, my activism is pretty lazy, I hafta admit. I mostly sit in front of this computer and spew stuff I believe in. This guy, Nick Triolo, is a teensy bit more energetic than I am. OK, he's a badass.

He was pissed about the development of an open-pit mine in a beautiful area of Mexico, so he did something about it. Something I could never do. He ran. Seventy miles in one day, to be exact.

He got lots of attention for the cause, and even made this film about it to spread the word. Doesn't it make you wonder what you could do for the causes you're passionate about?

headline: Why We Need A New Knee-Jerk Reaction When We Hear About People Getting Raped
lede:
In a perfect world, a victim of sexual violence would always be met with empathy. Of course, the world is not perfect and instead victims are often met with skepticism. People will question the validity of their victimization based on the nature of the victim, rather than the nature of the perpetrator or the crime.

This doesn't make sense, as Laci Greene demonstrates at 1:05, because we don't apply this sort of logic to any other crimes. But she really brings it home at 1:50 when she's goes over the five biggest problems with assigning blame to the victim instead of the perpetrator.

Oh, and next time you're tempted to say something like "what was she wearing?" instead say what Laci says at 4:07.

headline: 7 Delightful Posters That'll Probably Make You Realize Something's Missing At Your Day Job
lede:
A lot of people don't know what cooperatives are exactly, so here's the short of it: A cooperative is an organization or business that is jointly-owned and democratically-controlled by its members, all of whom share in the profits and benefits of the business. Sounds pretty great, right?

You might be thinking, "What's the difference between a cooperative and a corporation with shareholders?" Well, profit is the foremost driver of everything a standard corporation does, while cooperatives are people-centered — they put the social, economic, and even cultural needs of their members and communities at the center of their work.

What makes coops more sustainable and resilient than many conventional businesses is that members aren't just shareholders, they're stakeholders who actually have a say in company decisions and who have a deep interest in its long-term success. That's something the majority of people only wish they could say about their workplaces.

Below are the seven universally-recognized principles that guide cooperatives around the globe. As I read through them, I couldn't help but wonder how much better the world would be if more businesses were like this.

headline: The NFL May Get A Lot Of Things Wrong, But This Former Player Is 100% Right In His Rant On Spanking
lede:
Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson was briefly suspended from the team after admitting to repeatedly hitting his 4-year old son with a "switch" (a small, thin tree branch) and being indicted on child abuse charges as a result. The violent act as well as the NFLs response sparked a heated debate about corporal punishment, child abuse and football.

Former Minnesota Vikings player, NFL Hall of Famer and now sports commentator Cris Carter's contribution to that national conversation goes down as one of the clearest, rawest, and most personal reactions thus far.

headline: Do You Know About Tardigrades? They’re Impossibly, Insanely, Tough Little Creatures.
lede:

headline: Movies Treat 13-Year-Old Girls And 39-Year-Old Women The Same In One Incredibly Disturbing Way
lede:
Every time a new study about the state of women in movies (in front of the camera and behind the scenes) comes out, I cross my fingers and hope Hollywood has finally woken up to the realization that women make up 50% of the global population and should make up 50% of the film industry population too. BUT ALAS ... it is 2014 and that does not seem to be the case.

The good news is that when women direct and write movies, the number of female characters increases. The bad news, though, is that only 20% of writers and 7% of directors are women, which kinda/sorta/totally explains why only 31% of speaking roles in movies go to female characters. Even worse, female characters are 5 times more likely to have their appearance commented on in a film than male characters are, which means what speaking time female characters do get is often wasted discussing their appearance rather than the plot. *LOUD ANGRY SIGH*

If you found that as upsetting as I did, scroll to the bottom for a great quote by real life badass Hollywood heroine, Geena Davis, about one thing Hollywood can do to change things for the better — and not just in movies, either.

headline: Not Ready To Commit? How About Some Pets You Couldn’t Hurt If You Tried?
lede:
Tiny tardigrades, also called ‘water bears’, are just the most insanely tough creatures on earth. These dinky vegetarians have been flung into the chilling vacuum of space, stomped, frozen, and burned — they don’t care. It’s just downright hilarious how tough they are, and they’re everywhere: The highest mountains, deepest ocean floors, your back yard. Probably your skin.

We may worry about climate change and weapons of mass destruction. Them, not so much.

But he doesn't just sing for First Nations people — he sings for everyone keeping up with "the struggle."

headline: They Went Back To See What Global Warming Had Done, And Couldn’t Even Tell Where They Were Standing
lede:
I love this short film about the Rwenzori mountains of Uganda. They’ve been known for thousands of years as “the mountains of the moon” and as the legendary source of the Nile River. What makes this such a great video is how fantastically weird the mountains are, with multiple ecosystems, and animals that exist nowhere else. The filmmakers came chasing retreating glaciers they wanted to get pictures of before it was too late. And with the refreshing degree of respect they bring to their Bokonjo porters, it makes for a wonderful few minutes in a unique place being transformed by climate change.

You’ll hear about the mountains’ legend at :44, and be introduced to see some of its odd landscapes at 3:13. The filmmakers struggle with the mountain’s uncooperative weather before making some a startling discovery at 7:25 about what’s happened there.

lede: Let's get something out of the way up front: sexual violence is not gender specific. It took a few seconds for it to hit me: The poem's words are what the *fields* would tell if they could speak.

But once you realize that, and keep that in mind as you listen to the rest of the spoken word poem, the reality of what happens in the fields will hit you hard.
share_text: The Beatles sang 'Strawberry Fields Forever.' But I wouldn't want to be in *these* strawberry fields.

headline: The Suspicious Thing? Only People Who Weren't Black Were Suspicious Of Them.
lede:
I live in New York City, and I happen to be a black man as well. I was coming out of the subway the other day when I spied two cops (both caucasian) hanging around the exit. This is a semi-usual thing in the city, I believe they patrol stations randomly from time to time. But they both looked at me when I got out, and I immediately thought, "Well, this is when it happens to me. This is when i get stopped and frisked." So I looked at one of them like "Me, right?" and he gave me a bemused look as if to say " No, you don't look suspicious. Keep on walking." and then I realized I didn't look suspicious because I was coming back from a date, and was dressed nicely.

Ending the lives of men that look very similar to me is something I contend with every day, and with the recent death of Vonderrick Meyers, who was shot 17 times and allegedly was only holding a sandwich. I was inspired to make the following image after hearing the news.

headline: This Mom Was Tired Of Princesses. So She Did Something About It.
lede:
Professor Setsu Shigematsu, who is a professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department of University of California, Riverside, found her efforts at limiting her daughter's exposure to princess culture ineffective. lede:
I know it's popular to panic, and say "Shut it down! Shut it all down!" when it comes to air travel. Insulating ourselves won't stop the spread of Ebola. But now it has our attention, and we have to be smart about it. This may not be the popular sentiment, but the fact remains the only reliable way to prevent the spread of Ebola is by quelling it at its epicenter. That means putting our resources to work where they can make the most difference. That's gonna mean you and I caring about what happens with this disease overseas, supporting U.S. money and help being directed to West African Ebola treatment, and worrying a little less about wearing our full body latex to the airport. Are you ready now?

headline: Kids Today Are More Depressed Than They Were During The Great Depression. Here's Why.
lede:
When I first heard about how common it's becoming for some schools to withhold recess from kids as a disciplinary tool, my heart was heavy. Play is a very important part of childhood. I'm not even sure I realized how important until I heard this man, who makes his living studying play, talk about it.

Our kids are spending more time in classrooms and less time on the playground. They're spending more time in front of the TV, and less time in front of their houses, playing on the street. And while we all talk about how these things impact their physical health and lead to obesity and Type 2 diabetes, we're failing to recognize how we're making our kids mentally sick, too.
share_text: Our children are paying a very high price for our actions — actions that we can change.

headline: This Kid's Skin Falls Off If He Moves Wrong. So The Fact That He Cracks Jokes Is Kind Of Impressive.
lede: Epidermolysis Bullosa is a disease I had never heard of until today. 30,000 people in the United States today have it. It essentially makes your skin and organs extremely fragile. Children with it have their fingers slowly fused together into mitten shapes. Skin that is cut never heals. Families can spend as much as $14,000 a month on bandaging alone. Athletic and physical activities are out of the question. They are prone to skin cancer. And one of them happens to be friends with Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder. And so he started a foundation you should learn about. They're doing research that could impact 5000 rare genetic disorders impacting 10% of the globe's population.
share_text: He has a disease that some call 'diabolical' and yet he still grins like a mischievous angel.

headline: His Grandma Told Him A Pretty Amazing Story That I Think You'll Want To Hear If You Enjoy Breathing
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.
share_text: A letter to every science-denying human on the planet who thinks plugging your ears is a good idea.

headline: What Jim Carrey's Interpretive Dance SNL Sketch Can Teach Us About Halloween Microagressions
lede:
If you saw the Jim Carrey/Iggy Azaela episode of "Saturday Night Live" you saw the Halloween sketch in which Carrey and Kate McKinnon parodied Sia's interpretive dance "Chandelier" music video (if you didn't see it, you're about to). Don't get me wrong, their performances were great, but my favorite part of the sketch happened before those two even showed up on stage, when Vanessa Bayer's character was trying to figure out what her co-workers' costumes are supposed to be.

We’d all love to think that we don’t treat people differently based on their race, or gender, or body shape, or whatever — but the unfortunate truth is that we all do it a little bit sometimes. Halloween is supposed to be a time when we can all dress up as other people, characters, objects, and/or really bad puns. The beginning of this sketch really shows how, even when it comes to Halloween (or wearing costumes in general), things like race, gender, and/or body shape become the thing that we refuse to let people shed even when they’re pretending to be someone or something else.

headline: All Moms Are Different In Their Own Special Way, But Here Are Some That Are Finding Common Ground
lede:
I think of motherhood as the most incredible thing I never knew I wanted so much until I had it. Before I was a mom, I didn't understand what it felt like to experience true, unconditional love for another human being. And now that I do, I know it's pretty amazing.

headline: If You Bristle Every Time Someone Talks About 'Privilege,' This Is For You
lede: The term "privilege" is loaded for some people. I get it — it can cause feelings of guilt over something that isn't a favor you asked for. But what I LOVE about this series of posters from University of San Francisco is that it makes clear that what's necessary isn't guilt, but simply awareness. We didn't make the world this way, but we don't have to sit back and just be passive beneficiaries of inherent inequities, either. Just by being aware, you can start to make the world a tiny bit more just. Here are 6 types of privilege to be aware of, and a little primer on what we even mean by that.

headline: Got 7 Minutes To Be Wildly Inspired? Because This Is Some Seriously Good Stuff.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.

headline: Only 1 Country Does This Terrifying Thing To 13-Year-Olds. It's The U.S.
lede:
Wow. Human rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson gives a stunning talk about injustice in our criminal system. It's a heavy topic, and there's no way to dress it up as uplifting, but at least Stevenson's charisma and engaging stories make it incredibly mesmerizing.

He starts off slow with stories of his grandmother, but by 6 minutes in he's dropping facts about our prisons that many people would much rather ignore. And it just gets better and better — don't miss the hilarious story at 17:35 about the time he asked a judge to try his client as a rich white dude. And my favorite quote of the whole talk comes at 20:35: "The moral arc of the universe is long, but it bends towards justice." Chills, people, CHILLS!

headline: A Caribbean Kid Sat Down For Dinner With His Parents. And His Boyfriend. This Is How It Went.
lede:
In my dating life, I have a few moments that stand out to me. When I was 20, I literally kissed a guy in the summer when it started to rain on our first date. (I mean, you couldn't ask for a more Romantic Comedy starring YOU kind of moment, am I right?) When I was a junior in art college, I had my first serious boyfriend. So serious, that we met each other's parents over Christmas break. I met his in Brooklyn, and then the next week, over Christmas, he met mine in Washington DC.

The following poem I wrote after the experience of having him stay over my parents house. They're Haitian, very religious and quite homophobic, still — unfortunately. They love me, but the "being-gay-is-bad" mantra was driven into them when they were young and now they're elderly (both in their 70s).

I'm still pulling for 'em.

From a guy who's been on the receiving end of years of low-grade hate from family members (not all of them!), maybe think about how it feels to be on the other side of your discomfort with someone's life. And ask yourself why you feel so uncomfortable, maybe.

headline: The Truth About The Ferguson Case That Most People Won't Acknowledge
lede:
Some things I have learned:

Pro Publica recently did an in-depth analysis and found that black kids between the ages of 15-19 are 21 times more likely to be shot and killed by cops than white kids of the same age. That's an insane statistic. That's per capita, not actual numbers. If you are a black teenage boy, you have a 21x higher risk of being shot by police.

Also, in 2010, Federal prosecutors took 162,000 cases to a grand jury. You know how many DIDN'T go to trial? 6.

Also, Mike Brown's family will never get a state criminal trial to get justice for their son. And the testimony that denied them that right technically doesn't make any sense. Seriously, go read it.
share_text: If you say "But what about black-on-black crime?" I'm gonna have to roll my eyes.

headline: Have Long Hair? I Bet You're Sick Of Strangers Telling You To Do What This Toddler Just Did.
lede:

Her uncle gives her a haircut.

And then she gives a sick child her hair.

headline: 16 Years Ago, A Doctor Published A Study. It Was Completely Fake, And It Made Us All Sicker.
lede:
Once upon a time, a scientist named Dr. Andrew Wakefield published in the medical journal The Lancet that he had discovered a link between autism and vaccines. After years of controversy and making parents mistrust vaccines, along with collecting $674,000 from lawyers who would benefit from suing vaccine makers, it was discovered he had made the whole thing up. The Lancet publicly apologized and reported that further investigation led to the discovery that he had fabricated everything.

In the intervening years, millions have been spent on studying this further to see if there was anything that could connect autism and vaccines. This is what they found.

headline: This Doll Looks Exactly Like The Girl From The Hunger Games, And Means A Lot To Young Girls Actually
lede:
I have a very easy confession to make. I grew up with Barbie, and I loved braiding her hair.

She never factored into any storytelling I did (that was reserved for my music videos I directed using a camcorder and my sister and her friends — you should see my interpretation Weezer's 'Sweater Song' — a lot of sweaters were involved), but in the 90s, Barbie had super a cool minidresses and super long hair and I lovvvvved that about her.

She looked like this:

and she was ev-a-reee-thaaang.

I *still* want to be that Barbie, honestly.

So as much as I do love Barbie as a child of the 90s, seeing artist Noel Cruz flip the script on mass produced beauty ideals. He takes the face of, in this case, the Hunger Games Katniss Barbie,

If this doesn't point out the pointlessness of paying attention to the way large corporations view women (profiteers who don't think it's worth the time to make female (and male) look like THEMSELVES when there's money to be made) — I don't know what does.

Yeah, not every kid's gonna get a handpainted real-face Barbie. But every kid might see this and go — wait. There's value in looking real. And *that* is ev-a-ree-THANG.

excerpt: She doesn't just care about helping victims on TV.
headline: A Much-Loved TV Cop Speaks Out To Celebrate What Manhattan's D.A. Just Decided Regarding Rape Kits
lede:
Who doesn't love them some Olivia Benson? But did you know that Mariska Hargitay got so many letters from sexual abuse victims that she founded an organization to help them heal? And as a part of that work, she is involved with the community of advocates and activists who help change laws and attitudes toward sexual abuse in real life.

So when Manhattan's District Attorney announced recently that he'd allocate up to $35 MILLION in funding to help get through the backlog of rape kits that have never been tested, Mariska took to the stage to applaud that and, hopefully, inspire other jurisdictions to do the same.
share_text: This decision is a big darn deal.

excerpt: We talk a lot about them, but do we even know what they are?
headline: Every Person On Earth Is Supposed To Have These. But What Are They Exactly?
lede:
There are a lot of terms we throw around, but maybe we've forgotten the true meanings. If all you know about human rights is that a lot of people put those "=" bumper stickers on their cars, or make them their Facebook picture, you could probably use a refresher course.

And if your refresher course comes from 25+ brilliant minds who work hard to uphold our human rights? Bonus.

I especially appreciate what they say starting at 2:40 - just who are the people we need protecting from? And at 3:06 I feel encouraged to keep speaking up on social media platforms (I hope you do, too). At 4:12, a quick, eye-opening story about how it feels to be denied your human rights is all the reminder we should need to keep working on these issues.

lede:

In 2014, to change perceptions about American Indians, photographer Matika Wilbur believes have to update the kind of imagery we're looking at when we think of her race. It's a beautiful — and important — idea.

headline: These Kids Were Asked To Act Like A Famous Idol, And They Knocked It Out Of The Park
lede:
Eunique J. Gibson started the "Because of Them We Can" project in 2013 to honor African Americans who have been pioneers in their fields and to help children see all the possibilities that lie ahead of them. She does it in the coolest, cutest way -- by dressing kids up to emulate these trailblazers and photographing them.

I'll use Ms. Gibson's own words from another video to describe it: "It's about empowering these kids and injecting this new wave of self-esteem and self-worth by understanding what's already been done, what's being done, and what can be done."

It's been wildly popular, which means she's gonna keep expanding on the project, like making videos similar to the one here. I'm happily joining the growing list of people who are super excited to see what else she does next.

excerpt: The Daily Show hilariously embarrasses a rude old dude and then for the encore makes me cry when they find this amazing woman.
headline: One Of Putin's Homophobic Spokesmen Is Shamed On 'The Daily Show' And That's The Least Awesome Part
lede:
In the run up to the Sochi Olympics, there was uproar over Russia's awful anti-gay laws that were destroying lives and families. The Daily Show decided to head over to find out what the deal was and interviewed one of Putin's spokesmen. Said spokesman confirmed all their worst fears. So Jason Jones went onto the streets to find out more. And although he discovered 74% of Russians are anti-gay, he also found pockets of beautiful dissent. At 4:06, he asks the people that really matter, a bunch of LGBTQ Russians, why they don't just leave. At 5:40, he meets an amazing woman who actually makes me tear up a little. It doesn't even end with a joke.

If you live somewhere other than the USA, I've provided instructions on how to see the video at the bottom of the page. Because you deserve better than a media company's awful region restrictions.

But the part that really gets me is the companies out there that slip an unnecessary amount of it into their food products. And not just certain ones, like.. most of them. They do it because they know the affect it has on our minds, and therefore their annoying profits. Sneaky, sneaky.

headline: Baby Showers Usually Lead With: "It's A Girl!" Or "It's A Boy!" Here's Why That's A Problem

When we let go of the idea of what it means to be a girl or to be a boy, we allow our children to unleash their true selves and reach their full potential.

headline: Here Are Some Posters For The Men Who Tell Women What To Do Or What They Think Of Them In The Street
lede:
Every day women are harassed in the street simply by being a woman. Or in other words: every time we step out the house we run the risk of being shouted at, cat-called or assaulted usually in broad daylight. FUN!

Brooklyn based artist Tatyana Fazlalizadeh wanted to take women's voices and faces and plaster them big and bold in the very same places where this takes place. She's addressing gender based street harassment by taking a place where women feel uncomfortable and turning it into a place where we cannot be ignored through street art, and that is pretty awesome.

lede: In the United States, we have a lot of pride in country. And why not? We are an exceptional country indeed. Case in point: globally, we rank number one (USA! USA! headline: Malala's Father Explains His Daughter Is So Strong Because He Didn't "Clip Her Wings."
lede:
Ziauddin Yousafzai’s daughter Malala was shot by the Taliban in 2012 after she has just boarded a bus to school. Today, Malala is now recognised around the world as a global leader for women's rights ... at the age of 16.

Ziauddin explains in his TED talk how he was determined to raise his daughter to be strong, confident, and passionate. He stresses that the plight of millions of women could be changed if both men and women think differently and break against the norms of family and society.

His message gives an inspiring lesson for all of us — fathers, mothers, men, women — to hear.

headline: Kate Mara And Ellen Page's True Detective Spoof Makes Me Wish The Real Show Had Cast A Leading Lady
lede: I really loved the first season of True Detective. It made me see Matthew McConaughey as a serious actor, and I loved the story. I was planning to watch season two, but the casting announcement disappointed me something fierce. No female detective or a person of color in a leading role? I could overlook it for one season, but now it's clear the honchos just want to cater to what they perceive is the main demographic instead of making a wider tent. I think it's an unfortunate move, but these two fantastic actresses seem to have heard my frustration and made a parody to cheer me up. As silly as they're being in this video, it does actually help me visualize how great the show would be with one or more female leads. Take note, Nick Pizzolatto. Women make awesome detective characters, too.

headline: They Went Back To See What Global Warming Had Done, And Couldn’t Even Tell Where They Were Standing
lede:
I love this short film about the Rwenzori mountains of Uganda. They’ve been known for thousands of years as “the mountains of the moon” and as the legendary source of the Nile River. What makes this such a great video is how fantastically weird the mountains are, with multiple ecosystems, and animals that exist nowhere else. The filmmakers came chasing retreating glaciers they wanted to get pictures of before it was too late. And with the refreshing degree of respect they bring to their Bokonjo porters, it makes for a wonderful few minutes in a unique place being transformed by climate change.

You’ll hear about the mountains’ legend at :44, and be introduced to see some of its odd landscapes at 3:13. The filmmakers struggle with the mountain’s uncooperative weather before making some a startling discovery at 7:25 about what’s happened there.
share_text: I want to go to there.

headline: 3 Harmless Items Used To Justify Someone's Death
lede:
I live in New York City, and I happen to be a black man as well. I was coming out of the subway the other day when I spied two cops (both caucasian) hanging around the exit. This is a semi-usual thing in the city, I believe they patrol stations randomly from time to time. But they both looked at me when I got out, and I immediately thought, "Well, this is when it happens to me. This is when i get stopped and frisked." So I looked at one of them like "Me, right?" and he gave me a bemused look as if to say " No, you don't look suspicious. Keep on walking." and then I realized I didn't look suspicious because I was coming back from a date, and was dressed nicely.

Ending the lives of men that look very similar to me is something I contend with every day, and with the recent death of Vonderrick Meyers, who was shot 17 times and allegedly was only holding a sandwich. I was inspired to make the following image after hearing the news.
